label: Research step only: probability that the claim is misleading, realistic claims

settings.checkerModels: the pipeline's forced picks: Muse Spark 1.3 for search, writer and source verifier

probability.prompt:
You are a research agent that fact-checks claims made in podcasts, interviews, and articles. Use the web_search tool to find evidence.

## What you get
A single factual claim taken from a podcast, interview, or article, plus a short excerpt around it for context. The message shows them as:
  Text from Transcript: <excerpt>   (or "Text from Article:")
  Claim: <the claim>
Judge whether the claim is factually correct.

## Output format
Return JSON with two fields:
- findings: a dense research summary. Include the full https:// source URL inline next to each claim it supports — write out the complete link, never use footnote numbers, domain shortcuts, or citation markers.
- misleading_probability: your subjective probability, as a number from 0 to 1, that the claim is misleading in any way.

## Sourcing rules
- Include what each source says that's relevant.
- If the claim is not misleading, the findings can be brief — just explain why.

Respond with strict JSON only matching: { findings: string, misleading_probability: number }

The claim is broadly accurate as a description of the typical AFL-affiliated craft union, but it overgeneralizes if read to mean every AFL craft union enforced all three practices. EH.net’s overview of the 1920s U.S. economy says most craft unions required apprenticeships before workers could become journeymen, making skill and apprenticeship barriers to entry; it also describes the AFL as built around national unions’ exclusive jurisdictions (https://eh.net/encyclopedia/the-u-s-economy-in-the-1920s/). A historical account in the *Encyclopedia of U.S. Political History* says the AFL executive board defended boundaries between craft unions and exclusive representation of particular crafts (https://sk.sagepub.com/ency/edvol/embed/encyclopedia-of-us-political-history/chpt/american-federation-labor-1). But the AFL was a federation of autonomous unions, and practices varied: the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ 1929 handbook lists at least one AFL-affiliated union with no apprenticeship regulations (https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/publications/bls/bls_0506_1929.pdf). So the claim captures a real and characteristic pattern, especially around apprenticeship and jurisdiction, but “AFL craft unions” should not be taken as a universal statement about every affiliate.

The claim is broadly accurate for many AFL-affiliated craft unions, but it overgeneralizes if read as applying uniformly to all of them. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ 1925 *Handbook of American Trade-Unions* documents craft unions setting apprenticeship terms and limits: for example, some unions required a set apprenticeship before journeyman membership and capped apprentices relative to journeymen; the handbook also records unions with no apprenticeship system, showing the practice was not universal (https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/title/handbook-american-trade-unions-4034/fulltext). The handbook describes AFL’s 1907 “one craft, one union” policy and records jurisdictional disputes and efforts to consolidate unions representing the same or similar trades—evidence of formal trade-boundary protection, though not proof that every union behaved identically (https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/title/handbook-american-trade-unions-4034/fulltext). A later BLS handbook likewise records craft unions encouraging apprenticeship systems and regulating apprentice numbers (https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/title/handbook-american-trade-unions-4139/fulltext). In short, apprenticeship regulation, entry limits in some trades, and defense of craft jurisdiction were real and recurring features, but “AFL craft unions” is too sweeping without qualification.

Substantially accurate, with a qualification: this describes a common feature of AFL-affiliated craft unions, not a uniform rule imposed by every affiliate. The historical study *Between Craft and Class* reports that, in late-19th-century metalworking, union rules and customs limited the number of apprentices and that skilled work was often restricted to apprenticed craftsmen or union members; it also documents disputes over work assigned across craft boundaries (https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/between-craft-and-class-skilled-workers-and-factory-politics-in-the-united-states-and-britain-1890-1922.html). The U.S. Department of Labor’s history describes the AFL as founded by craft-union leaders seeking to protect their jurisdictions (https://www.dol.gov/general/aboutdol/history/chapter4). A 1926 U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics handbook records particular AFL-affiliated unions requiring completed apprenticeships for membership and imposing apprentice limits, while also showing that rules varied by union (https://fraser.stlouisfed.org/files/docs/publications/bls/bls_0420_1926.pdf). Thus apprenticeship controls, restricted access to particular skilled work, and protection of trade jurisdictions are well supported; “jealous guarding” is rhetorical phrasing, and the sentence is somewhat overgeneralized if read to mean every AFL craft union applied all these practices.

The claim is too broad to verify as stated because it gives no date or traveler category. A 1977 Soviet customs rule said belongings crossing the border were generally admitted duty-free “within personal needs” and separately listed categories with specific quantity limits; it did not establish an unlimited right to take any amount of every item (https://law.tks.ru/document/2606). In the version of the 1989 Soviet customs regulation available here, the enumerated export prohibitions do not name condoms, but that list alone does not prove that no other customs or personal-needs rules applied (https://legalacts.ru/doc/polozhenie-o-porjadke-propuska-i-deklarirovanija-tovarov/). Contemporary reporting also documents that the USSR imposed restrictions on exporting certain consumer goods in 1989, illustrating that export rules changed over time; it does not establish a condom-specific limit (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/business/1989/01/06/trade-war-within-soviet-bloc-escalates-disrupting-travel/). So the evidence found is consistent with there being no specific numerical cap on condoms under the cited rules, but it does not substantiate the absolute claim that there was no restriction on how many a person could take out of the Soviet Union.

The claim is too broad to verify without the traveler’s date and status. Soviet customs rules approved on December 15, 1977 did not specify a numerical limit for condoms, but they did not allow unlimited personal luggage: goods had to be within “personal needs,” defined by the circumstances of the trip, and personal items had to correspond in kind and quantity to its purpose and duration. Source: https://law.tks.ru/document/2606. From September 15, 1989, a separate decree banned certain categories of consumer goods from export by specified travelers and imposed a 100-ruble-per-person value ceiling; its prohibited list included medicines and sanitation/hygiene articles, though it does not name condoms specifically. Source: https://lawrussia.ru/texts/legal_346/doc346a268x887.htm. So the evidence supports a narrower statement—there may have been no condom-specific numerical quota in some circumstances—not the categorical claim that there was no restriction on how many condoms a person could take out of the USSR.

The claim is too absolute. The USSR Ministry of Foreign Trade’s customs rules of December 15, 1977 did not specify a separate numerical quota for condoms in the provisions reviewed, but they did impose general quantity limits: for personal trips, items had to be in quantities necessary for the stay abroad (clause 20); for permanent relocation abroad, belongings were allowed only “within personal needs” (clause 45). The rules also said items exceeding their established quantities would not be admitted across the border (clause 42). Source: https://law.tks.ru/document/2606. Thus, there may have been no condom-specific cap, but that is not the same as there being no restriction at all. Because the excerpt does not give the date or type of departure, the exact rule applicable to the anecdote cannot be determined.

The claim accurately reflects what was said in the transcript: on CNN’s October 12, 2026, “One World,” retired Colonel and CNN military analyst Cedric Leighton said that some elements of the intelligence community view the Houthis as relatively independent, while others see them as more aligned with Iran (https://transcripts.cnn.com/show/ow/date/2026-10-12/segment/01). The broader issue is consistent with a September 2024 congressional hearing statement by a CSIS expert: it described Iran’s network as a loose consortium, said the Houthis should not be viewed simply as extensions carrying out Tehran’s orders, and characterized their relationship with Tehran as comparatively loose and unstructured (https://www.congress.gov/118/meeting/house/117655/witnesses/HHRG-118-FA13-Wstate-LordJ-20240919.pdf). That testimony supports the substance of the independence-versus-alignment debate, but does not independently document a split within the U.S. intelligence community. Thus the claim is supported as an accurate report of Leighton’s characterization; the asserted internal intelligence-community disagreement is not publicly verified by these sources.

The claim is plausible, but the specific assertion that different parts of the U.S. Intelligence Community hold opposing views is not clearly established by the public sources reviewed. In Senate testimony, then-DNI Avril Haines said the Houthis pursue domestic political advantage and produce some weapons themselves, while also receiving Iranian assistance—an assessment compatible with both local agency and close ties (https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CHRG-118shrg60835/html/CHRG-118shrg60835.htm). The Intelligence Community’s 2025 Annual Threat Assessment characterized the broader “axis of resistance” as a “loose consortium of like-minded” actors; a Congressional Research Service report notes that experts debate how much autonomy Iran-backed groups have (https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2025-05-22_R47321_78886ef22e8ac264c34c001b2915590f48893507.html). These sources support the existence of differing interpretations of Houthi-Iran ties, but do not independently confirm that the disagreement is specifically between elements within the U.S. intelligence community.

The claim accurately summarizes what retired U.S. Army intelligence officer Robert Leighton said in a CNN interview transcript dated October 12, 2026: he called Houthi independence from Iran a “bone of contention” within the intelligence community, saying some elements viewed the Houthis as relatively independent while others saw them as more aligned with Iran (https://transcripts.cnn.com/show/ow/date/2026-10-12/segment/01). This verifies the attribution, but the transcript does not identify the agencies or provide independent evidence of their internal assessments.
